analysis.one_liner: Opens shipping to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico to competition by waiving Jones Act rules on monopoly routes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was referred to a House subcommittee in February 2021 and sat there with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires ships carrying goods between US ports — including routes to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico — to be built in the US, mostly US-owned, and mostly US-crewed. This bill would waive those rules on any route where fewer than three independent companies compete, letting foreign-built and foreign-crewed ships carry goods there. The goal is to break up shipping monopolies and lower the shipping costs baked into island prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other island territories, who pay a shipping premium on nearly everything they buy because the Jones Act shields a small set of carriers from cheaper foreign competition. Retailers and importers serving those markets would also gain. The exemption is targeted: it only kicks in on routes without at least three genuinely independent operators, so it aims squarely at monopoly and duopoly routes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new exemption to the Jones Act for carriage on noncontiguous trade routes, unless at least three unrelated operators each carry at least 20% of the volume on that route — in other words, relief applies only where real competition is already absent.

On the exempted routes, foreign-built, foreign-owned, and foreign-crewed vessels could carry goods, ending the legal exclusivity that lets one or two carriers set rates on a route — the standard mechanism by which shipping competition is expected to lower costs for island consumers and businesses.

Because Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico depend on ocean shipping for virtually all inbound goods, freight rates flow directly into grocery, retail, and construction prices there; the bill targets exactly those routes.

analysis.who_pays: The established Jones Act carriers that hold protected noncontiguous routes (a small group of US operators) would lose their legal exclusivity and face foreign-flagged competition. US shipyards would lose captive demand for expensive US-built vessels, and some US-flag seafaring jobs could shift to foreign crews. The main gains go to island consumers, so the cost is concentrated in a small, protected industry.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act shipping lines and US shipyards

drawbacks.text: Weakening Jones Act requirements reduces demand for US-built ships and US-crewed vessels, which could cost shipyard and merchant-marine jobs — working-class jobs — and shrink the US-flag fleet and mariner pool the military draws on in emergencies.

The exemption hinges on a market-structure test: if three operators each carry 20% of a route, even at high prices, no exemption applies, so concentrated but nominally competitive routes would stay protected and savings would not reach every route.
There is no guarantee savings from foreign competition would be fully passed to consumers; importers and retailers could retain part of the reduction before it reaches the shelf price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of people in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico, lower freight costs would be a real, ongoing gain in cost of living. The costs are real but concentrated: protected carriers lose excess profits, shipyards lose premium US-built orders, and some mariner jobs are at risk. The bill's trigger — exempting only routes without three independent operators — is narrower than full repeal and limits the disruption. The tradeoff is a genuine one, but it pits the cost of living of millions of island residents against a small set of protected companies and their suppliers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, and it stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case of Hawaii introduced the Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act on January 13, 2021.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, the committee with jurisdiction over maritime law.
On February 4, 2021, it was referred to the subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation — the last recorded action it ever received.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Jones Act carriers and US shipyards that depend on the current rules kept their protected noncontiguous routes untouched, while residents of Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico continued paying the shipping premium the exemption would have targeted.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; the only sponsor it ever had.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair, Rep. Peter DeFazio, D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 13, 2021, and over the full two-year Congress never held a hearing or markup or advanced it to the floor.

against.name: Jones Act shipping operators
against.what_they_did: The US-flag carriers that hold these routes have long opposed Jones Act exemptions as a bloc, and no exemptions of this kind advanced in the committee.

sides.party_line_note: One House Democrat sponsored the bill, no one else — in either party — cosponsored it, and no committee or floor votes were ever recorded, so no partisan split ever became visible.

industries.note: These operators hold legally exclusive rights to carry goods on US noncontiguous routes and charge accordingly; the bill opens any route served by fewer than three independent operators to foreign-flagged competition, ending their rate-setting power on the routes that matter most to island residents.

Shipyards depend on Jones Act buyers, who must purchase far costlier US-built vessels; every exempted route shrinks that captive demand. Shipyard jobs are real, but the industry's protected revenue comes at the expense of island consumers.

industries.industry: US merchant mariners and maritime labor
industries.note: The US-crew requirement underpins protected seafaring jobs on noncontiguous routes; opening those routes to foreign-crewed vessels puts some of those jobs at risk even as it lowers costs for consumers.
